params.question: In the motorcyclist with a comminuted patellar fracture and a lateral tibial plateau depression, which clinical finding is the strongest indicator of developing compartment syndrome?

answers.text: Swelling of the knee with the leg held in 20 degrees of flexion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Knee swelling and a flexed posture reflect the fracture itself and the resulting haemarthrosis, not rising pressure within a muscle compartment.

answers.text: Pain on passive dorsiflexion of the ankle with a tense leg

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Pain elicited by passively stretching the muscles within a closed compartment — here, the anterior compartment — combined with tense swelling is the hallmark early sign of rising compartment pressure.

answers.text: Numbness along the lateral aspect of the leg

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lateral leg numbness suggests common peroneal nerve injury from the tibial plateau fracture, not necessarily compartment syndrome.

answers.text: Inability to straighten the leg against gravity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Loss of active knee extension reflects disruption of the extensor mechanism from the patellar fracture, not compartment pressure.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the case findings. Among the options listed, pain on passive dorsiflexion with a tense compartment is the hallmark of compartment syndrome — the other findings point to the fractures themselves or to nerve injury.
Well done. Pain on passive stretching of the affected compartment's muscles is the earliest and most reliable clinical sign of compartment syndrome.

interactions.label: A palpable dorsalis pedis pulse rules out compartment syndrome in the leg.

params.question: A palpable dorsalis pedis pulse rules out compartment syndrome in the leg.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is a critical clinical pitfall. Pulses disappear only after compartment pressure exceeds systolic blood pressure — long after irreversible ischaemic damage has begun. Pain on passive muscle stretching is the earliest and most reliable sign. Never rely on pulse status alone to exclude compartment syndrome.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Exactly right — this is a dangerous misconception. Peripheral pulses persist until compartment pressure exceeds systolic blood pressure, by which time irreversible muscle and nerve damage has already occurred. The earliest sign is pain out of proportion to the injury, especially on passive stretching of the affected compartment's muscles.

interactions.label: Which finding classifies an open tibial fracture as Gustilo-Anderson Grade IIIC?

params.question: Which finding classifies an open tibial fracture as Gustilo-Anderson Grade IIIC?

answers.text: A skin wound larger than 10 cm with moderate contamination

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wound size alone helps distinguish lower grades. A large wound without vascular compromise does not reach Grade IIIC.

answers.text: Extensive bone exposure requiring a soft tissue flap for coverage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes Grade IIIB, where periosteal stripping and soft tissue loss necessitate flap coverage, but the vessels remain intact.

answers.text: Multiple fracture fragments with significant bone loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Comminution and bone loss indicate high-energy injury but do not by themselves define Grade IIIC. The grading hinges on vascular status.

Correct. Grade IIIC is specifically defined by arterial damage that requires surgical vascular repair. These injuries demand a multidisciplinary team — orthopaedic, plastic, and vascular surgeons working together.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall from the narration that the Gustilo-Anderson classification ranges from Grade I (a small, clean wound) up to Grade IIIC, defined specifically by vascular injury needing surgical repair.
Correct. Vascular injury requiring repair is what elevates an open fracture to Grade IIIC — the most severe category in the Gustilo-Anderson system.

interactions.label: A true Jones fracture of the fifth metatarsal often requires surgical fixation r

params.question: A true Jones fracture of the fifth metatarsal often requires surgical fixation rather than conservative management because:

answers.text: The peroneus brevis tendon displaces the fracture fragment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Peroneus brevis avulsion causes the pseudo-Jones fracture at the styloid tip — a different and typically benign injury that heals well with a firm shoe or boot.

answers.text: The fracture site lies in a vascular watershed zone with poor blood supply

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The true Jones fracture occurs 1.5–2 cm distal to the styloid process, in a watershed area between two vascular territories. This compromised blood supply impairs healing and frequently necessitates screw fixation.

answers.text: The fracture extends into the metatarsophalangeal joint surface

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A Jones fracture is at the metadiaphyseal junction, well away from the joint surface. Intra-articular involvement is not the reason for surgical intervention here.

answers.text: The fifth metatarsal bears the greatest load during the push-off phase of gait

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The first and second metatarsals bear more load during push-off. The Jones fracture's poor healing is due to its vascular watershed location, not excessive mechanical loading.

overallFeedback.feedback: The critical distinction is anatomical: the true Jones fracture sits in a vascular watershed zone 1.5–2 cm distal to the styloid, with poor blood supply. This distinguishes it from the more benign pseudo-Jones avulsion at the styloid tip.
Well done. The watershed blood supply at the metadiaphyseal junction is the key reason the true Jones fracture heals poorly and often requires surgery.

interactions.label: Which feature of fat embolism syndrome is considered the most distinctive and sp

params.question: Which feature of fat embolism syndrome is considered the most distinctive and specific to this condition?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Respiratory distress is common to many conditions — pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, and ARDS can all present with tachypnoea and hypoxaemia. It is part of the triad but not the most distinctive feature.
Neurological changes such as confusion occur in numerous settings — head injury, hypoxia, sepsis, and drug effects. While part of the triad, they are not specific to fat embolism.

answers.text: Petechial rash on the chest, neck, and conjunctivae

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Petechiae distributed across the chest, neck, and conjunctivae are the most distinctive sign of fat embolism syndrome. This distribution pattern, in the context of a recent long bone fracture, is virtually pathognomonic.

Fever and tachycardia are non-specific systemic responses seen in infection, inflammation, and many post-operative states. They are minor criteria in the Gurd and Wilson system, not the hallmark feature.

overallFeedback.feedback: The classic triad comprises respiratory distress, neurological changes, and a petechial rash. Of these three, the narration identifies petechiae (on the chest, neck, and eyes) as the most distinctive sign of fat embolism syndrome.

Correct. The petechial rash — on the chest, neck, and conjunctivae — is the most distinctive clinical sign of fat embolism syndrome and completes the classic triad alongside respiratory distress and neurological changes.
